## Teaching philosophy

At a time when environmental problems are of great concern, the biological sciences are expected to produce solutions to overcome the crisis. However, as a teacher of biology, I regard the attempt to turn biology into a mere "solution-making" machine as miseducative for students. Instead, I see biological education as the cultivation of an appreciation for nature and an education in scientific processes.

Appreciation of nature gives people a real sense of stewardship. I believe in an organic, yet hidden, connection between humans and the natural world. To help students re-establish that connection, I give them opportunities to interact with nature and develop their own sense of appreciation through lectures on natural history, field trips, and discussions. I also use myself as an example of how one can connect with one's surroundings. I encourage students to spend time looking at nature and finding something that interests them, so that their appreciation of nature, rather than my authority, becomes the driving force of their education.

I portray biology as science. My role as a teacher is to give students ways to go into nature, ask questions, and carry out experiments. Drawing on my research experience, I use class and lab time to expose students to current methods in biology, and I work with students who need to develop new approaches that better fit their questions. It is a chance for students to question and experience scientific processes, rather than to produce specific, if not right, answers to problems. A strong foundation in biology will not only contribute to our long-accumulating body of knowledge but also give future society the incentives and the means to protect the place we live.
